item.title: ADULT. Turn Political Disillusionment Into Their Most Focused Electropunk Yet on Kissing Luck Goodbye
item.description:
The Detroit duo ADULT. — Nicola Kuperus and Adam Lee Miller — have been making electropunk records for 25 years, long enough that the term has accumulated stylistic baggage they've usually managed to sidestep. Their tenth studio album, Kissing Luck Goodbye, released March 27 on Dais Records, is their clearest statement in some time: ten tracks, no padding, no ambient interludes softening the blows. Produced with Nolan Gray (who also co-produced their last record), the approach here is notably more direct — louder, more compressed, Kuperus's vocals pushed further to the front of the mix.

The sonic approach has always been the duo's most identifiable trait: drum machines at post-industrial tempos, synth lines that operate as rhythm instruments as much as melodic ones, and vocals that land somewhere between singing and declaration. What shifts on Kissing Luck Goodbye is the ratio of dancefloor utility to sonic abrasion. Tracks like R U 4 $ALE and Freaks have warehouse-ready kick patterns underneath cut-up vocals and game-show samples — they would work in a DJ set while remaining unmistakably ADULT. records. No Song goes the other direction: machinelike, near-monolithic, the most overtly industrial thing they've recorded in recent years, with a layering strategy that prioritizes texture accumulation over melodic resolution.

The album is dedicated to Douglas McCarthy of Nitzer Ebb, and that lineage sits near the surface throughout. But the comparison isn't reductive: where Nitzer Ebb's aggression was physical and quasi-militarist, ADULT.'s has always been queasy and ironic, using the forms of power electronics and synth-punk to document powerlessness rather than perform strength. The political disillusionment that runs through the lyrics isn't the kind that resolves into rallying cries — it's the kind that produces laughter, and laughter as a response to the absurd is the album's consistent emotional register. Destroyers, the four-and-a-half-minute closer, sits with grim endurance rather than any cathartic peak.

That choice to not provide release — to maintain tension rather than resolve it into a breakdown or triumphant refrain — separates the record from contemporary electro-punk that uses the same reference points. The Wax Trax\! adjacency is real, and reviewers have noted Public Image Ltd and Siouxsie and the Banshees as touchstones, but Kissing Luck Goodbye doesn't feel like catalog retrieval. The production has been updated without being overproduced: the low-end is cleaner than earlier ADULT. records without losing the deliberate roughness in the midrange where most of the textural action happens.

What works best about the album is how it deploys track length as a variable rather than a constant. Most of the ten tracks run between two and four minutes, keeping the record from overstaying its welcome, but a few push into territory where repetition becomes the point — where the loop doesn't resolve because the thing it's describing doesn't resolve. That's a harder structural choice than it looks, and the fact that it mostly works testifies to how well Kuperus and Miller understand what their music is actually doing versus what it superficially resembles.

The vinyl is limited to 700 copies. For listeners who know ADULT.'s catalog, this is the record where accumulated pressure finds its most coherent form. For newcomers: a good entry point precisely because it's so confident in what it is. No experimental detours, no genre-testing moments. Just a very good electropunk album made by people who've spent a long time figuring out exactly what that means.

item.title: Dave Huismans Deepens the ex_libris Narrative With an Unhurried Third Release
item.description:
Dutch producer Dave Huismans re-emerged in June 2025 after roughly seven years of near-silence under his ex_libris alias, and with his third release in the series — dropped March 27, once again through Rush Hour distribution — the project's logic is becoming clearer. ex_libris 003 is a three-track 12-inch (25 minutes total) that operates with the same unhurried intentionality as its predecessors: hand-stamped vinyl, custom-printed colored sleeve, limited to the point of selling out almost immediately.

Listeners who followed Huismans as 2562 (Tectonic, then eventually his own Cosmic Bridge label) or as A Made Up Sound (Clone, Delsin) will recognize the lineage but not find a simple retrieval of those approaches. His earlier 2562 work was rooted in the dubstep-adjacent strain of bass music that dominated the UK in the late 2000s — heavy low-end, halftime rhythms, a specific attention to spatial depth that came directly from how that music was mixed for large PA systems. A Made Up Sound pushed into more abstract leftfield techno territory. ex_libris draws on both, but the tempo has slowed and the architecture is more patient.

The A-side, #6-27 (untangled), runs over ten minutes and is described by Boomkat as a rough-around-the-edges, spirited 4/4 beatdown epic — which undersells how much structural work is happening in that runtime. The track doesn't fill its length with variation for variation's sake; it's closer to a study in accumulation, where each element that's added or subtracted from the mix changes the pressure dynamics of the whole. The kick pattern stays close to deep house convention but the surrounding textures are drier and more abrasive, which creates a persistent low-level friction that keeps the track from sitting comfortably in any single genre pocket.

The B-side tracks — #7 (cosmic ripples) at 9:25 and #31 (reprise) at just under five minutes — move into what the same reviewers have called ambient-dub dematerialisation, which is useful shorthand for the way Huismans uses reverb and filter decay not as atmosphere-generators but as structural tools. The decay time on individual elements is calibrated to keep the room sounding active even when the density drops; what you're left with is something that has the spatial qualities of a well-designed listening experience but retains enough rhythmic residue to feel tethered to club context. #31 (reprise) functions as a coda, paring back to near-nothing over five minutes in a way that makes the preceding material feel denser in retrospect.

The numbering system across all three releases — tracks titled with numbers from what appears to be a larger archive — suggests that Huismans is treating ex_libris as a selective publication project rather than a conventional release schedule: pulling finished pieces from a body of work and issuing them when they cohere into a sequence. Whether that framing is literal or just good mythology is hard to say, but it aligns with how the music actually sounds — deliberately curated rather than goal-directed, as if the priority is internal coherence rather than market timing.

The vinyl is sold out, digital available. For producers working in leftfield house and dub techno, ex_libris 003 is the kind of record that rewards close attention to how the mix decisions function rather than how the tracks flow. Huismans has always been a producer's producer in that sense — his work is better understood as an argument about what these genres could prioritize than as an accessible entry into them. This is not a criticism. It's why the series matters.
